routes.label: Encode signs as +-1 and reduce the pyramid to the bottom product

question:
In a sign pyramid a cell gets a “+” if the two cells below it have the same sign, and it gets a “-” if the two cells below it have different signs. The diagram below illustrates a sign pyramid with four levels. How many possible ways are there to fill the four cells in the bottom row to produce a “+” at the top of the pyramid?

[Figure 1](figures/2018_AMC_8_Q19_question_fig1.svg)
solution:
Replace a \(+\) sign by the number \(+1\), and a \(-\) sign by \(-1\). The pyramid rule then becomes multiplication: equal signs multiply to \(+1\), while different signs multiply to \(-1\).

Label the bottom values \(a,b,c,d\). The row above is \(ab,bc,cd\). The next row has values

\[
(ab)(bc)=ab^2c=ac,\qquad (bc)(cd)=bc^2d=bd,
\]

because both possible values \(+1,-1\) have square \(1\). Thus the top value is \((ac)(bd)=abcd\).

This product is positive exactly when an even number of the four bottom signs are negative. There is one way to have no negatives, \(4\cdot3/2=6\) ways to choose the two negative positions, and one way to have four negatives. The total is

\[
1+6+1=\boxed{8},
\]

choice \(\boxed{\text{C}}\). Encoding a rule with numbers can reveal what information survives repeated steps.
